affinity

/uh-FIN-ih-tee/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Affinity means a natural, often immediate liking or connection between people, or a natural inclination toward an activity or idea.

On her first day at the firm, Dana felt an instant affinity for her mentor, who laughed at the same odd jokes and kept the same gloriously messy desk.

Example

Miguel discovered his affinity for mystery stories in fourth grade and has read at least one whodunit a month ever since.

Nobody assigned Miguel those books — he felt a natural pull toward the genre the moment he found it. An affinity can point toward an activity or interest, not just toward a person.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rapport: Rapport is the warm, easy flow two people fall into once conversation clicks — a quality of the interaction itself. An affinity is the underlying pull that draws you toward a person or activity in the first place. Rapport describes how the exchange feels; affinity names the attraction behind it.

kinship: Kinship is the feeling of being fundamentally alike — you recognize yourself in the other person. An affinity does not need that likeness: it is a natural, sometimes instant liking that can spring up between people who share almost nothing. Kinship rests on sameness; affinity only needs the pull.

penchant: A penchant is a strong habitual liking for an activity or thing — you show it by returning to the thing again and again. An affinity can point at people as well as pastimes, and it can appear in a single moment rather than build through habit.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

aversion: a strong dislike or desire to avoid

antipathy: a deep-seated dislike

Where it sits · how strong the pull toward it is

interest → affinity → passion

interest vs. affinity: Interest is weaker than affinity — you can be mildly interested in dozens of things, but an affinity is a genuine pull that feels natural and personal.

passion vs. affinity: Passion is stronger than affinity — a passion consumes your time and energy, while an affinity may stay a quiet, comfortable draw.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — af-: to, toward (a form of Latin ad- that changes spelling before f)

Root — fin: border, boundary (Latin finis)

Suffix — -ity: the state or quality of

Put it together: Affinity is literally 'the state of bordering on' — in Latin, affinis described neighbors whose lands shared a boundary, and later people connected by marriage. From 'sharing a border' the word grew into sharing a natural connection.

Use the root in a new word: finite: The club's budget was finite, so they set firm boundaries on what each event could spend.

Word Building

Word Choice

Neutral — personal, everyday register

Watch the prepositions: you feel an affinity for an activity or person ('an affinity for music'), and an affinity with or between people ('an immediate affinity between the two cousins'). Don't confuse it with fidelity, another word in this unit: an affinity is a spontaneous liking that can appear in a single conversation, while fidelity is loyalty that proves itself over a long time.
